name: API Styles
intent: Choose between REST, GraphQL and gRPC by what each one costs in round trips, payload size and flexibility for the clients that call it.
scenario: A mobile app needs a screen that shows a customer's name, their last three orders and the items in each order. The backend has separate user, order and item data.
problem: An API is a contract between teams, and its shape decides how many network calls a screen needs, how much unused data travels, how easily clients can ask for something new and how hard the contract is to change. No single style is best for every caller.

howItWorks.title: REST: resources with URLs and standard verbs
howItWorks.text: Each thing (user, order, item) has a URL, and you use GET, POST, PUT and DELETE on it. Responses are cacheable, any HTTP tool can call it, and it is easy to understand. The server decides the shape of each response, so a screen that needs data from several resources makes several calls, and each response may carry fields the client ignores.

howItWorks.title: GraphQL: the client describes the data it wants
howItWorks.text: There is one endpoint. The client sends a query naming exactly the fields it needs across related objects, and the server returns just that in one response. This removes over-fetching and extra round trips, at the cost of harder caching, a query language to secure, and care so that one query cannot become very expensive.

howItWorks.title: gRPC: typed remote procedure calls over HTTP/2
howItWorks.text: The contract is a protobuf file that defines methods and message types, and code is generated for both sides. Messages are compact binary, calls are fast, and streaming is built in. It suits service-to-service calls; browsers cannot call it directly without a proxy, and the binary format is harder to inspect by hand.

howItWorks.title: Count the round trips and the bytes
howItWorks.text: A request costs at least one network round trip (tens to hundreds of milliseconds on mobile). Fetching related data one request after another multiplies that. Smaller payloads help slow connections. Measure what the real screens need before choosing.

howItWorks.title: Mixing styles is normal
howItWorks.text: Many systems use gRPC between internal services, REST for public integrations that need simplicity and caching, and GraphQL as a gateway for their own front ends. The right question is who the caller is and what they need to be able to change without asking the backend team.

pros: GraphQL: clients fetch exactly what a screen needs in one trip
gRPC: fast, small messages, strict generated contracts, streaming
Each can be the best fit for a different kind of caller
cons: REST: over-fetching and many round trips for screens that join data
GraphQL: caching, rate limiting and security are harder, and expensive queries must be bounded
gRPC: weak browser support and less human-readable
Running several styles means more to learn and operate
whenToUse: REST for public APIs, simple CRUD and anything that benefits from HTTP caching
GraphQL when many different clients need different slices of related data
gRPC for internal service-to-service calls where speed and strict contracts matter
whenNotToUse: GraphQL for a small API with one client, where a few REST endpoints are simpler
gRPC for a public API that browsers and third parties must call easily
REST alone when screens need data stitched from many resources over slow networks
pitfalls: Choosing by fashion instead of by the callers' real needs
GraphQL queries with no depth or cost limit, which let one client overload the server
REST endpoints that mirror database tables, forcing clients to make many calls
Changing a protobuf field number or a GraphQL field meaning, which breaks old clients silently

quiz.question: A mobile product page needs the product, its price, 3 reviews and the seller name. Today it makes four REST calls on a 300 ms mobile network and each response carries many unused fields. Which change fits this problem best?
options: Switch the four calls to gRPC from the phone, since binary messages are smaller and faster
Add a GraphQL layer so the screen asks for just those fields at once
Add an HTTP cache header to each response, so that repeat visits are served locally
Merge the four resources into one large REST endpoint that every client then uses
quiz.explanation: GraphQL lets the client name the fields across related objects in one trip. Caching does not remove the extra round trips, and a single big endpoint over-fetches for every other client.

quiz.question: A company has 40 internal microservices that call each other thousands of times per second. Teams keep breaking each other with undocumented JSON changes. Which choice is the best fit for these internal calls?
options: GraphQL with one endpoint per service, so each team can expose its own schema
REST with a wiki page that lists each response shape and is kept up to date by the owners
Server-sent events on every call so that any changes are pushed to the other services
gRPC with shared protobuf files, giving a typed, generated contract
quiz.explanation: gRPC gives compact messages, speed and a strict contract that breaks at build time. A wiki page does not enforce anything, and GraphQL is aimed at varied client queries.

quiz.question: A public GraphQL API has no limits. A partner sends a query that nests users, their friends, the friends' friends and their posts, and the database is saturated for ten minutes. What should the team add?
options: Limits on query depth and cost, with rate limits that count that cost
A switch to REST with one endpoint per table, so that each call has a fixed shape
A larger cache in front of the GraphQL server, so repeated heavy queries are served quickly
A rule that only GET requests are allowed, so that clients can only read and never write
quiz.explanation: A GraphQL query lets the client choose its own cost, so the server must bound depth and complexity. A cache helps only for repeated queries, and switching styles does not fix the root cause.
